label: Generic elevation claim
why: The phrase signals premium positioning without giving the reader a concrete reason to believe it.
action: Delete it or replace it with a specific service, standard, credential, outcome boundary or proof point.

label: Thoughtfully-designed filler
why: This adjective phrase often describes intent rather than something the reader can verify.
action: Show the actual design choice or delete the claim.

label: Difference without evidence
pattern: \b(designed to feel different|a different kind of|feels? unlike)\b
why: Difference is asserted instead of demonstrated.
action: Replace the claim with the observable difference, or remove it.

label: Journey / experience staging
pattern: \b(your next experience starts here|begin your journey|transformative journey|curated journey)\b
why: Staging language delays the action and is portable across unrelated brands.

label: Portable premium adjective
why: These words can be valid, but they are often used where a concrete noun or proof point would do more work.
action: Ask what this word means here. Keep it only if the surrounding sentence proves it.

label: Not-just / but construction
why: This contrast frame is frequently overused in generated marketing copy.
action: State the stronger clause directly unless the contrast genuinely changes meaning.

label: Unanchored superlative
why: A superlative without a comparison or source creates a trust debt.
action: Add verifiable evidence or remove the claim.

label: Generic CTA
pattern: \b(explore services|explore experience|discover crown & core|discover more|learn more|get started)\b
why: Generic CTA labels make the reader infer what happens after the click.
action: Use the actual action: book, compare, see pricing, read treatment details, or request an audit.
